::: {.oneline}
Since an expectation value evolves the state forwards and then back again, the
time ordering that makes diagrams work has to run along a path doubling back on
itself.
:::

## Short answer

Scattering theory asks a question with a beginning and an end, in which
something comes in from far away and something goes out. We only ever need to
propagate forwards, from the initial state to the final one, and the whole
diagrammatic machinery is built on this.

Condensed matter usually asks a different question. There is no out state, since
we want the value of an observable in the state the system is in right now. We
must therefore start from the known state, evolve forwards to the moment of
measurement, apply the observable, and then evolve *back* to where we started.
The evolution appears twice, once in each direction.

If we insist on ordering operators along an ordinary time axis, this breaks the
bookkeeping that allows a complicated expectation value to be expanded into
diagrams. The repair is to stop thinking of a single axis and to use instead a
path running forward to late times and then returning. Ordering along that path
restores the structure, and the diagram rules come back essentially unchanged.

The price we pay is that a single time argument now carries an extra label,
namely which branch of the path it sits on. This is indeed where the several
different Green functions come from (retarded, advanced, and those describing
occupation). They are not independent objects, but the same function read off
different combinations of branches.

## Why it works this way

In equilibrium there is a shortcut. The state we must return to is the ground
state, and adiabatic arguments guarantee that it is the same one we started
from, up to a phase, so that the backward branch can be absorbed. Out of
equilibrium this guarantee is lost, since the system genuinely does not return,
and the contour is therefore no longer optional.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: contour ordering and components

Expectation values take the form

$$
\langle \hat O(t) \rangle = \Big\langle\,
\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal C} \exp\!\left[-\frac{i}{\hbar}\oint_{\mathcal C} d\bar t\;
\hat H(\bar t)\right] \hat O(t) \,\Big\rangle ,
$$ {#eq-contour-ordering}

with $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal C}$ ordering along the contour $\mathcal C$ rather
than along real time. Placing the two arguments on the forward or backward
branch generates the components $G^{<}, G^{>}, G^{R}, G^{A}$, subject to
$G^{R} - G^{A} = G^{>} - G^{<}$, so that only two are independent. Perturbation
theory, Wick's theorem and Dyson's equation all survive with real time replaced
by contour time.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The contour is a mathematical trick with no physical content."** It encodes
  the physical difference between asking for a transition amplitude and asking
  for an expectation value.
- **"Keldysh is only for driven systems."** It also covers steady-state
  transport, in which the state is stationary but not an equilibrium one.
